linkages: All variables are linked at the individual level across years in the Statistics Denmark registers; the paper names no identifier or linkage key.
Retirees in 2016 are linked to their own 1999-2015 pension-contribution and wage-income history to compute average contribution rates.
Retirement income growth is predicted by sorting individuals above age 59 who retired between 1996 and 2001 into income cohorts and applying those cohorts' average income growth to the 2016 retirees.

sample.universe: Section 3: all individuals who began receiving public pensions in Denmark in 2016 while aged 60 or older (43,993). Section 4: all individuals living in Denmark aged between 25 and 40 in 1996.
sample.unit_of_observation: Section 3: the individual (one observation per 2016 retiree). Section 4: the individual x period, where the base period is the 1996-98 average and the post period the 2011-13 average. Contribution rates and the Figure 6 LPM use a person-year panel.
selection_rules: Section 3 (Table 1): start from 43,993 individuals who began receiving public pensions in 2016 at age 60 or older.
Exclude self-employed individuals (3,389), whose salary income is not directly observable so consumption cannot be reliably imputed.
Exclude individuals involved in housing transactions in 2016 (884).
Exclude individuals with negative imputed consumption in the year before retirement (4,388).
Exclude individuals with annual income below 7,500 DKK (849).
Exclude individuals with income above the 99th income percentile (445).
Exclude immigrants (2,538), because full public pension benefits require 40 years of residency.
This leaves 34,383; excluding 1,480 individuals with missing income information leaves a final sample of 32,903.
Tables 6 uses 30,837 of these; Table 7 uses the 3,017 who contributed on average below 1 percent of wage income to mandatory pensions between 1999 and 2015.

Section 4: individuals aged 25-40 in 1996; those who did not pay anything into labour market pension schemes for five years or more are excluded; individuals below 25 are excluded to avoid graduating students and those above 40 to avoid retirement at the end of the sample.

Section 4 keeps only the top 30 percent (treatment, average annual increase in the mandatory contribution rate above 0.51 percentage points) and bottom 30 percent (control, below 0.14 percentage points) of the 1996-2010 contribution-growth distribution.

When averaging contribution rates, year-person observations more than three standard deviations above the mean are dropped (mandatory above 32 percent, private above 18 percent of wage income; above 26 percent for the private rate in the Table 7 subsample); these are about 2.5 percent of the year-person observations.
sample.period: 1995-2016 (register coverage); contribution rates averaged 1999-2015; Section 4 treatment period 1996-2010 with outcomes compared between 1996-98 and 2011-13
sample.n_observations: 32,903 individuals in Table 5; 30,837 in Table 6; 3,017 in Table 7; 749,722 / 749,228 / 755,070 / 736,053 observations in Table 9 columns (1)-(4); 522,868 person-year observations in the Figure 6 LPM; 4,487,987 individuals in the Table 3 population column.
sample.n_individuals: 32,903 retirees in 2016 (Section 3); 197,367 treatment and 197,550 control individuals in 1996, and 190,867 and 190,429 in 2010 (Section 4).

construction_notes: Consumption is imputed following Leth-Petersen (2010) as c_t = y_t - ΔA_t + ΔD_t, where y_t is disposable income (total income including labour income, social welfare benefits, unemployment benefits, child benefits, capital income and inheritance, less interest and tax payments), A_t is liquid assets (bank deposits including the balance of private pension schemes) and D_t is total debt (mortgage, bank and other debt), all at end of year t; i.e. disposable income minus net savings.
Stock and bond holdings are deliberately excluded from liquid assets because active investment decisions cannot be separated from unrealized gains and losses.

Target wealth is the wealth sufficient to cover the present value of a constant retirement consumption stream equal to 90 percent of the consumption level one year before retirement, over remaining life expectancy, at a 2 percent discount rate.

Life expectancy is differentiated by sex (in 2016, 18.8 years for a 64-year-old man and 21.6 for a woman) and adjusted by income quantile following Kallestrup-Lamb et al. (2022): plus/minus 2.5 years for women and plus/minus 3.5 years for men in the highest/lowest income quantile.

Retirement income from public transfers and other sources is not observed; it is predicted from the yearly percentage change in disposable income of individuals above age 59 who retired between 1996 and 2001, sorted into cohorts by income at retirement, and discounted at 2 percent.
Pension wealth is reported pre-tax; a uniform 40 percent tax rate is assumed, consistent with the Danish Economic Council (2023).
Savings gap_i = Target wealth_i - Total wealth_i (Eq. (1)); total wealth is wealth outside pension accounts + wealth in pension accounts + the present value of predicted future income.

Contribution rates are the annual amount paid into mandatory or private pension schemes as a fraction of wage income; the average rate for the retirement cohort is taken over 1999-2015 (Table 4 instead says 1995-2015).

Average annual contribution rates to labour market pensions are 8.28 percent with a standard deviation of 4.14 percent; to private pensions 2.26 percent with a standard deviation of 4.18 percent (p. 129).

Section 4 treatment and control groups are defined by the average annual increase in the mandatory contribution rate 1996-2010; the treatment group's rate rises from about 3 to about 12 percent of income, the control group's from about 9 to about 11 percent.
Reported wage income in Table 8 is net of contributions to the mandatory pension scheme.
Education is Statistics Denmark's level 1-4 classification (1 = primary school or less, 2 = secondary or vocational, 3 = short/medium/long higher education, 4 = PhD); levels 3 and 4 are combined.

claims.statement: Individuals who contributed to a mandatory (labour market) pension scheme in the year before retirement are about 5 percentage points less likely to have a positive savings gap at retirement than those who did not.

definition.value: Dummy variable D_i^man equal to 1 if individual i contributed to a mandatory (labour market / occupational) pension scheme in the year before retirement, and 0 otherwise.

timing.value: Measured in 2015, the year before retirement in 2016.

definition.value: Dummy equal to 1 if the individual has a positive savings gap and 0 otherwise. The savings gap is Savings gap_i = Target wealth_i - Total wealth_i (Eq. (1)). Target wealth is the wealth at retirement sufficient to cover the present value of a constant consumption stream equal to 90 percent of the individual's consumption level one year before retirement over remaining life expectancy, discounted at 2 percent, with life expectancy differentiated by sex and adjusted by income quantile. Total wealth is wealth outside pension accounts plus wealth in pension accounts plus the present value of predicted future income.

timing.value: Measured at retirement in 2016; pre-retirement consumption is taken from 2015, the year before retirement.

units.value: change in the probability of having a positive savings gap (probit partial effect at the mean), contributors relative to non-contributors

magnitude.interpretation: 'individuals who contributed to a mandatory pension scheme in the year before retirement are approximately 5 percentage points less likely to end up with a positive savings gap'

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the control vector (gender, age, marital status, homeowner, education level, public employment status, income decile, log gross wealth and log pension wealth), the pension-contribution measure is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of the savings gap. The paper never asserts this; it reports its estimates as associations ('correlates', 'associates with').
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. The paper motivates the control vector (e.g. it cites Kolsrud et al. (2024) for 'the importance of controlling for age in our regressions') but offers no balance test, pre-trend or placebo.

key_assumptions.assumption: Target wealth, and hence the savings gap, is computed under assumed values the paper imposes rather than observes: a 90 percent pre-retirement consumption replacement target, a 2 percent discount rate, sex- and income-quantile-adjusted life expectancy, a uniform 40 percent tax rate on pension wealth, and retirement income predicted from the 1996-2001 retirement cohorts.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sensitivity analyses: Figure 5 traces the share with a positive savings gap across thresholds; footnote 7 states the results go through with a 0 percent discount rate; alternative 3-, 5- and 10-year pre-retirement consumption benchmarks give 14.2, 14.1 and 14.0 percent.

threats_discussed: Self-employed individuals are excluded because their consumption cannot be reliably imputed and because they are less likely to have a mandatory pension scheme, which 'could bias our results'.
Individuals involved in 2016 housing transactions are excluded because extreme recorded wealth changes would bias imputed consumption.
Immigrants are excluded because full public pension benefits require 40 years of residency, so their present value of future income would be overestimated.
Public transfers and other retirement income are not observed and are predicted from the income streams of individuals who retired between 1996 and 2001.
Pension wealth is observed pre-tax; a uniform 40 percent tax rate is assumed.
Stock and bond holdings are excluded from liquid assets in the consumption imputation because active decisions cannot be separated from unrealized gains and losses.
robustness_checks: Logit and OLS versions of the Table 5 regressions (Tables A3 and A4, online appendix).
Logit and OLS versions of the Table 7 regressions (Tables A6 and A7, online appendix).
Alternative target-wealth thresholds (Figure 5 and Figure A1): 10.3 percent at an 80 percent threshold and 21.3 percent at a 100 percent threshold.
Alternative pre-retirement consumption benchmarks using the average over the 3, 5 and 10 years before retirement: 14.2, 14.1 and 14.0 percent have a positive savings gap (Table A1).
A 0 percent discount rate instead of 2 percent (footnote 7, p. 127): 'Our results go through with a discount rate of 0 percent.'
Excluding all households with substantial bond and/or stock holdings (footnote 6, p. 126; Appendix A).

evidence.how: The paper states on p. 131 that 15.0 percent of individuals retiring in 2016 have a positive savings gap. Table 5 is estimated on that same final sample of 32,903 retirees (Table 1), so 0.150 is the mean of the dependent variable; it is written as a proportion to match the units of the probit partial effects.
The table prints no p-value. The significance stars on this coefficient (***) are read against the table note's legend reproduced in the cited quote.
The paper prints no confidence interval for this estimate; only a standard error in parentheses.
The paper prints no standard deviation of the dependent variable for this estimation sample.
The paper names no Danish register or register variable code; it says only that the data are register-based data accessed through Statistics Denmark.

timing.value: Averaged over the yearly contribution rates from 1999 to 2015, i.e. up to the year before retirement.

definition.value: Dummy equal to 1 if the individual has a positive savings gap and 0 otherwise. The savings gap is Savings gap_i = Target wealth_i - Total wealth_i (Eq. (1)). evidence.how: The paper states on p. 131 that 15.0 percent of individuals retiring in 2016 have a positive savings gap. Table 5 is estimated on that same final sample of 32,903 retirees (Table 1), so 0.150 is the mean of the dependent variable; it is written as a proportion to match the units of the probit partial effects.
The table prints no p-value. The significance stars on this coefficient (***) are read against the table note's legend reproduced in the cited quote.
The paper prints no confidence interval for this estimate; only a standard error in parentheses.
The paper prints no standard deviation of the dependent variable for this estimation sample.
The paper names no Danish register or register variable code; it says only that the data are register-based data accessed through Statistics Denmark.

value.normalisation: The two participation dummies of Eq. (2) are replaced by the individual's average 1999-2015 contribution rate to mandatory and to private pensions; the effect is per 1 percentage point of the rate and is reported as a partial effect at the mean.

value.claimed_domain: other settings similar to Denmark, i.e. countries with comparable high-mandatory-contribution pension systems
boundary_conditions: countries where other pension systems dominate are explicitly left to future research

anchor_quote.text: Specifically, individuals with an average contribution rate to mandatory pensions that is 1 percentage point higher are, on average, 0.25 percentage points less likely to have a positive savings gap.

claims.statement: The average 1999-2015 contribution rate to private pensions has no statistically significant relationship with the probability of a positive savings gap.

definition.value: The individual's average annual contribution rate to private pension schemes, computed from the yearly contribution rates between 1999 and 2015. Year-person observations more than three standard deviations above the mean (private contribution rates above 18 percent of wage income) are excluded as extreme outliers.

timing.value: Averaged over the yearly contribution rates from 1999 to 2015, i.e. up to the year before retirement.

definition.value: Dummy equal to 1 if the individual has a positive savings gap and 0 otherwise. The savings gap is Savings gap_i = Target wealth_i - Total wealth_i (Eq. (1)). Target wealth is the wealth at retirement sufficient to cover the present value of a constant consumption stream equal to 90 percent of the individual's consumption level one year before retirement over remaining life expectancy, discounted at 2 percent, with life expectancy differentiated by sex and adjusted by income quantile. Total wealth is wealth outside pension accounts plus wealth in pension accounts plus the present value of predicted future income.

timing.value: Measured at retirement in 2016; pre-retirement consumption is taken from 2015, the year before retirement.

units.value: change in the probability of having a positive savings gap per 1 percentage point higher average annual contribution rate (probit partial effect at the mean)

magnitude.interpretation: 'no statistically significant relationship is observed between the private average contribution rates and the likelihood of not saving enough'

key_assumptions.assumption: Target wealth, and hence the savings gap, is computed under assumed values the paper imposes rather than observes: a 90 percent pre-retirement consumption replacement target, a 2 percent discount rate, sex- and income-quantile-adjusted life expectancy, a uniform 40 percent tax rate on pension wealth, and retirement income predicted from the 1996-2001 retirement cohorts.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sensitivity analyses: Figure 5 traces the share with a positive savings gap across thresholds; footnote 7 states the results go through with a 0 percent discount rate; alternative 3-, 5- and 10-year pre-retirement consumption benchmarks give 14.2, 14.1 and 14.0 percent.

threats_discussed: Self-employed individuals are excluded because their consumption cannot be reliably imputed and because they are less likely to have a mandatory pension scheme, which 'could bias our results'.
Individuals involved in 2016 housing transactions are excluded because extreme recorded wealth changes would bias imputed consumption.
Immigrants are excluded because full public pension benefits require 40 years of residency, so their present value of future income would be overestimated.
Public transfers and other retirement income are not observed and are predicted from the income streams of individuals who retired between 1996 and 2001.
Pension wealth is observed pre-tax; a uniform 40 percent tax rate is assumed.
Stock and bond holdings are excluded from liquid assets in the consumption imputation because active decisions cannot be separated from unrealized gains and losses.
robustness_checks: Logit and OLS versions of the Table 5 regressions (Tables A3 and A4, online appendix).
Logit and OLS versions of the Table 7 regressions (Tables A6 and A7, online appendix).
Alternative target-wealth thresholds (Figure 5 and Figure A1): 10.3 percent at an 80 percent threshold and 21.3 percent at a 100 percent threshold.
Alternative pre-retirement consumption benchmarks using the average over the 3, 5 and 10 years before retirement: 14.2, 14.1 and 14.0 percent have a positive savings gap (Table A1).
A 0 percent discount rate instead of 2 percent (footnote 7, p. 127): 'Our results go through with a discount rate of 0 percent.'
Excluding all households with substantial bond and/or stock holdings (footnote 6, p. 126; Appendix A).

definition.value: Dummy equal to 1 if the individual has a positive savings gap and 0 otherwise. The savings gap is Savings gap_i = Target wealth_i - Total wealth_i (Eq. (1)). timing.value: Measured at retirement in 2016; pre-retirement consumption is taken from 2015, the year before retirement.

units.value: first-stage (selection-equation) estimate for the dummy equal to 1 if the individual has a positive savings gap; the table note does not say whether these are index coefficients or partial effects

Stock and bond holdings are excluded from liquid assets in the consumption imputation because active decisions cannot be separated from unrealized gains and losses.

claims.statement: Among 2016 retirees with almost no mandatory pension contributions, contributing on average 0-3 percent of wage income to private pensions is associated with a higher probability of a positive savings gap, relative to contributing zero.

definition.value: Dummy equal to 1 if the individual's average 1999-2015 contribution rate to private pension schemes falls in the bucket 0-3 percent of wage income, and 0 otherwise. The reference category is the group that contributed on average 0 percent of their wage to private pension schemes.

timing.value: Averaged over the yearly contribution rates from 1999 to 2015, i.e. up to the year before retirement.

definition.value: Dummy equal to 1 if the individual has a positive savings gap and 0 otherwise. The savings gap is Savings gap_i = Target wealth_i - Total wealth_i (Eq. (1)). Target wealth is the wealth at retirement sufficient to cover the present value of a constant consumption stream equal to 90 percent of the individual's consumption level one year before retirement over remaining life expectancy, discounted at 2 percent, with life expectancy differentiated by sex and adjusted by income quantile. Total wealth is wealth outside pension accounts plus wealth in pension accounts plus the present value of predicted future income.

timing.value: Measured at retirement in 2016; pre-retirement consumption is taken from 2015, the year before retirement.

units.value: change in the probability of having a positive savings gap (probit partial effect at the mean) relative to the group that contributed on average 0 percent of wage income

magnitude.interpretation: 'nor when examining the four contribution buckets in column (3) except for a contribution rate below 3 percent'

definition.value: Dummy equal to 1 if the individual has a positive savings gap and 0 otherwise. The savings gap is Savings gap_i = Target wealth_i - Total wealth_i (Eq. (1)). Target wealth is the wealth at retirement sufficient to cover the present value of a constant consumption stream equal to 90 percent of the individual's consumption level one year before retirement over remaining life expectancy, discounted at 2 percent, with life expectancy differentiated by sex and adjusted by income quantile. Total wealth is wealth outside pension accounts plus wealth in pension accounts plus the present value of predicted future income.

claims.statement: Individuals whose mandatory pension contribution rate increased the most between 1996 and 2010 saw consumption grow 3.8 percentage points less than individuals whose contribution rate was stable, comparing 1996-98 with 2011-13.

definition.value: Interaction D^treat * D^post in Eq. (3). D^treat indicates the treatment group: individuals whose average annual increase in the mandatory contribution rate between 1996 and 2010 was in the top 30 percent of the distribution, i.e. above 0.51 percentage points per year; the control group is the bottom 30 percent, below 0.14 percentage points per year. The treatment group's contribution rate rose from about 3 percent of income in 1996 to about 12 percent in 2010, the control group's from about 9 to about 11 percent. D^post indicates the post-treatment period.

timing.value: Treatment measured over 1996-2010; the base-period observations are the 1996-98 per-individual averages and the post-treatment observations the 2011-13 averages.

definition.value: Natural logarithm of average imputed consumption. Consumption is imputed from register income and wealth data as c_t = y_t - ΔA_t + ΔD_t, where y_t is disposable income, A_t liquid assets (bank deposits including the balance of private pension schemes) and D_t total debt, i.e. disposable income minus net savings. The regression uses the 1996-98 per-individual average for the base period and the 2011-13 average for the post period.

timing.value: 1996-98 average vs 2011-13 average

units.value: log points of average consumption; the paper reads the coefficient as 3.8 percentage points of consumption growth

The paper never names the assumption.

claims.statement: At the paper's benchmark threshold of 90 percent of pre-retirement consumption, 15.0 percent of individuals retiring in Denmark in 2016 have a positive savings gap - i.e. 85 percent have saved enough - and the share rises with the assumed threshold.

treatment.label: Assumed target-wealth threshold (percent of pre-retirement consumption)

definition.value: The normative replacement threshold used to define target wealth: the level of retirement consumption, as a percentage of the individual's consumption one year before retirement, that target wealth must finance over remaining life expectancy at a 2 percent discount rate. The paper's benchmark is 90 percent, following Battistin et al. (2009); Figure 5 traces the threshold from 100 percent down to 0.

timing.value: Applied to the consumption level one year before retirement (2015) and to wealth at retirement (2016)

outcome.label: Fraction of individuals with a positive savings gap (percent)

definition.value: The share, in percent, of individuals retiring in 2016 whose savings gap (Eq. (1): target wealth minus total wealth, where total wealth includes wealth outside pension accounts, wealth in pension accounts and the present value of predicted future income) is positive.

threats_discussed: Self-employed individuals are excluded because their consumption cannot be reliably imputed and because they are less likely to have a mandatory pension scheme, which 'could bias our results'.
Individuals involved in 2016 housing transactions are excluded because extreme recorded wealth changes would bias imputed consumption.
Immigrants are excluded because full public pension benefits require 40 years of residency, so their present value of future income would be overestimated.
Public transfers and other retirement income are not observed and are predicted from the income streams of individuals who retired between 1996 and 2001.
Pension wealth is observed pre-tax; a uniform 40 percent tax rate is assumed.
Stock and bond holdings are excluded from liquid assets in the consumption imputation because active decisions cannot be separated from unrealized gains and losses.
